title: My Toddler Screamed "Daddy, Down!" While We Played Airplane and Pointed at the Top of Our Cabinet. What I Found Up There Made My Blood Run Cold
fb_text:
I Was Playing Airplane With My Daughter When She Suddenly Screamed and Pointed at the Top of Our Closet. What I Found Up There Made My Blood Run Cold

Ellie, my three-year-old daughter, has one game she loves more than any other.

Airplane.

Every night before bed, I lift her high above my head and race around her room while she stretches out her arms and pretends to fly.

She is crazy about it.

My wife always warns me I'll hurt my back, but honestly, that never stops me.

Ellie is growing up fast. Soon I won't be able to hold her like that anymore.

Every one of these moments is special.

On Tuesday, Ellie was even more excited than usual.

We normally play airplane only in her room, but that night she wanted to fly through the whole house.

"Please, Daddy! One more flight!"

My wife's shift was running late, so it was just the two of us.

I lifted her as high as I could and marched down the hallway making loud airplane noises.

She giggled so hard she could barely breathe.

Past the bathroom, around the kitchen, and into the living room we went.

I asked where we were headed.

"To the moon!" she shouted.

We were both laughing.

Near the tall storage cabinet, Ellie suddenly went quiet.

"Daddy! Down!"

I figured she was being silly.

"Turbulence, Captain?"

"No! Daddy, down!"

The fear in her voice made me put her down at once.

She clung to my leg and hid her face in my jeans.

I didn't know what to think. Ellie had never been afraid during airplane before.

"Sweetheart, what's wrong? Did the ceiling fan scare you?"

She shook her head.

"No, Daddy. I'm scared of what's on top of that closet."

I looked up but saw nothing unusual.

The cabinet, which my wife brought from her mom's house, holds blankets, games, and decorations. It takes up the whole wall, almost as tall as the ceiling. Because of my height, I had never once checked the top of it.

When I asked Ellie what she saw, she only pointed.

I told her to stay by the couch and went to get a chair from the kitchen.

I set it down, climbed up, and what I saw on top nearly made me fall off.

Continue reading in the first comment.

One More Flight

"Please, Daddy! One more flight!"

My wife's shift was running late, so it was just the two of us. I lifted Ellie as high as I could and marched down the hallway making loud airplane noises. She giggled so hard she could barely breathe. Past the bathroom, around the kitchen, and into the living room we went.

I asked where we were headed.

"To the moon!" she shouted.

We were both laughing.

"Daddy! Down!"

Near the tall storage cabinet, Ellie suddenly went quiet.

"Daddy! Down!"

I figured she was being silly. "Turbulence, Captain?"

"No! Daddy, down!"

The fear in her voice made me put her down at once. She clung to my leg and hid her face in my jeans. Ellie had never been afraid during airplane before, and I didn't know what to think.

"Sweetheart, what's wrong? Did the ceiling fan scare you?"

She shook her head. "No, Daddy. I'm scared of what's on top of that closet."

I looked up but saw nothing unusual. The cabinet, which my wife brought from her mom's house, holds blankets, games, and decorations. It takes up the whole wall, almost as tall as the ceiling. Because of my height, I had never once checked the top of it. When I asked Ellie what she saw, she only pointed.

What Was Waiting Up There

I told her to stay by the couch and went to get a chair from the kitchen. I set it down in front of the cabinet, climbed up, and looked over the edge.

Through a thick layer of dust, a pair of glass eyes stared straight back at me.

I nearly lost my balance. Lying on its back, wrapped in yellowed lace, was an old porcelain doll with a cracked cheek and a faded painted smile. Its eyes were wide open and fixed on the ceiling. Seen from below, it was invisible. But a little girl lifted high into the air, flying right past the top of the cabinet, had come face to face with it.

My heart was pounding. Next to the doll sat a small rusty tin box, tied shut with a ribbon that had once been pink.

I let out a long, shaky breath and almost laughed at myself. It was only a doll. But I understood right away why Ellie had screamed. To a three-year-old, a staring face in the dark above her head was terrifying.

I carefully lifted the doll and the tin down. Ellie peeked out from behind the couch, still holding on to a cushion.

"It's okay, sweetheart," I told her. "Look. It's just an old doll. Nobody is up there anymore."

She studied it for a long moment. "She looks sad, Daddy."

I hadn't expected that. I looked at the cracked little face again, and she was right. It did look lonely.

A Secret From Grandma's House

When my wife finally came home, tired from her long shift, she found the two of us sitting on the living room floor with the dusty doll between us.

She went completely still.

"Where did you find that?" she whispered.

I told her about the airplane game, about Ellie's scream, and about the top of the cabinet. My wife sat down slowly and picked up the doll as if it might break.

"This was my mother's," she said, her eyes filling with tears. "She got it when she was a little girl. I thought it was lost years ago. After she passed, we looked everywhere for it."

She opened the rusty tin with trembling fingers. Inside were a few faded photographs and a handful of folded letters in her mother's handwriting. Some were addressed to my wife. Her mom had apparently tucked them away to give her one day and then simply forgotten about them, or never found the right moment.

We sat there for a long time while she read. I just held her hand. Ellie climbed into her lap, forgetting all about her fear.

"Is the doll still sad, Mommy?"

My wife smiled through her tears. "I think she was just waiting for someone to find her."

Bringing Her Home

The next weekend, we cleaned the lace and gently wiped the dust from the doll's face. My wife found a small shelf in our bedroom, at a height where Ellie could see her without fear, and that is where the doll sits now. Ellie named her Grandma Rose, and she waves to her every morning.

As for the letters, my wife reads one every Sunday evening. She says it feels like having her mother back at the kitchen table for a few minutes.

And Ellie still wants to play airplane every single night. We just fly a little differently now. Before takeoff, we always check the top of the cabinet.

Sometimes the things that frighten our children turn out to be the very things that lead us back to the people we love. I'm grateful my daughter was brave enough to say something, and that I was listening.
